title: What Actually Happens in a Recession
sources: NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee: a recession is 'a significant decline in economic activity that is spread across the economy and that lasts more than a few months' (depth, diffusion, duration) — nber.org/research/business-cycle-dating
NBER business cycle reference dates: Great Depression Aug 1929 – Mar 1933 (43 months); Great Recession Dec 2007 – Jun 2009 (18 months); COVID recession Feb 2020 – Apr 2020 (2 months)
NBER / Congressional Research Service IF10411: 12 postwar cycles (1945–2020) average contraction 10.3 months, average expansion 64.2 months
BEA: real GDP fell in Q1 and Q2 2022 (initial estimates −1.6% and −0.9% annualized); NBER did not declare a recession. BLS: unemployment 3.6% in June 2022 (CRS IF12774, Dallas Fed 2022)
BLS: unemployment rate peaked at 10.0% in October 2009; payroll employment fell by about 8.7 million (Jan 2008 – Feb 2010) — BLS Spotlight 'The Recession of 2007–2009'

BLS: unemployment rate 14.8% in April 2020 (revised), highest since data began in 1948; about 22 million jobs lost in March–April 2020 — BLS blog 'Looking Back on the 2020 U.S. Labor Market', CRS R46554
S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index: ≈27% decline from 2006 peak to 2012 trough
Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy on September 15, 2008
Federal Reserve: federal funds target range cut to 0–0.25% on Dec 16, 2008 and on Mar 15, 2020
CBO: American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009 ≈ $787 billion at passage; CARES Act (March 2020) ≈ $2.2 trillion
Great Depression: unemployment ≈ 24.9% in 1933 (BLS historical estimate, via FDR Library / CRS R40655)

Federal Reserve Bank of New York, 'The Yield Curve as a Predictor of U.S. Recessions' (10-year minus 3-month spread); FRED series T10Y3M: inverted Oct 25, 2022 – Dec 13, 2024 with no recession declared
S&P 500: fell ≈57% from Oct 9, 2007 to Mar 9, 2009; regained its 2007 closing high in March 2013 (S&P Dow Jones Indices)
BLS Employment Situation, August 2026: unemployment rate 4.1% (released Sept 4, 2026) — context only

beats.text: Dave sells couches at a big furniture store. Business is good. But this morning, his boss said one scary word. Recession.
Dave has heard that word before. Now look at this. In twenty twenty, America lost about twenty two million jobs. In just two months.
The unemployment rate jumped to fourteen point eight percent. The highest since records began in nineteen forty eight.
And wait, it gets weirder. Most people don't even know what a recession actually is.
Spoiler: it's not just two bad quarters.
Today: what a recession really is, the chain reaction that spreads it, and how Dave can get ready before it hits.
So what is a recession? Let's start simple.
The economy is everything we all make and buy. Couches, haircuts, pizzas, apps. Add it all up for a whole country, and you get a number called G D P.
When G D P grows, the economy is healthy. When it shrinks, something is wrong.
Most people think a recession means G D P shrinks for two quarters in a row. That's six months. Nope. That's just a rule of thumb.

In America, the official call is made by a group of economists at a research center called the N B E R. They say a recession is a big drop in economic activity, spread across the economy, lasting more than a few months.
They look at many things. Jobs. Income. Spending. Factory output. Not just G D P.
Here's proof. In twenty twenty two, G D P shrank two quarters in a row. But unemployment stayed at just three point six percent. People kept working. So the N B E R said: not a recession.
Think of it like a doctor. One high temperature doesn't mean you're sick. The doctor checks everything.
So how does a recession actually spread? It's a chain reaction.
Here's the secret. One person's spending is another person's paycheck.
When Dave's neighbor Bob buys a couch, that money pays Dave's salary. Dave spends it on pizza. And that pays the pizza guy.
Now imagine something scares people. Prices jump, or a bank fails, or a virus appears. Bob gets nervous. He keeps his old couch.
The store sells fewer couches. So the boss cuts hours. Or lets someone go.
Now that worker has less money. So they buy less pizza. So the pizza shop lets someone go too.
It's like a line of dominoes. Less spending leads to layoffs. Layoffs lead to less spending. And round and round it goes.
And big stuff falls first. Cars, houses, and yes, couches. When people get scared, a new couch is the first thing they skip. Gulp.
Let's look at two real recessions. First, two thousand eight.
In the early two thousands, banks gave home loans to almost anyone. Even people who couldn't really afford them.
Everyone believed house prices only go up. So people borrowed more and more.
Then prices started falling. Across America, home prices dropped by about twenty seven percent. Many people owed more than their house was worth. They stopped paying.
And those bad loans were packed inside investments owned by banks all over the world. It was like a Jenga tower. Pull out one block, and the whole thing wobbles.
Big banks got into deep trouble. One giant, Lehman Brothers, collapsed in September two thousand eight.
The recession lasted eighteen months. America lost about eight point seven million jobs. And unemployment peaked at ten percent, in October two thousand nine.
Now twenty twenty. This one was totally different.
No bad loans. No bubble. Just a virus. To slow it down, shops, restaurants, and offices closed almost overnight.
It was like someone hit the pause button on the whole economy.
In March and April alone, about twenty two million jobs disappeared. Restaurants and hotels were hit hardest.
Unemployment shot to fourteen point eight percent in April. Way higher than in two thousand nine.
But here's the surprise. It was also the shortest recession in American history. Just two months. From February to April.
Deep, but quick. Like a car that slams the brakes, then speeds off again.
So when the dominoes start falling, who tries to stop them? Two teams.
Team one: the Federal Reserve. America's central bank.
The Fed cuts interest rates, so borrowing gets cheaper. In both two thousand eight and twenty twenty, it cut rates almost to zero.
Cheaper loans mean people and companies borrow and spend again. The dominoes start standing back up.
The Fed can also create new money to buy bonds. Remember the duck? Yes. Money from nothing. Quack.
Team two: the government. It pays unemployment benefits, so people who lose their job can still buy food. And pizza.

It can also spend big. In two thousand nine, Congress passed a stimulus plan of about eight hundred billion dollars. In twenty twenty, the CARES Act was about two point two trillion. Many families got checks in the mail.
Critics say this adds to the national debt, and can push prices up later. Supporters say doing nothing would hurt far more. That's a political question. Now you know the tools.
Here's the good news Dave needs to hear. Recessions end.
Since the end of World War Two, America has had twelve recessions. On average, each one lasted about ten months.
And the good times in between? On average, more than five years.
Think of it like weather. Storms are real, and they hurt. But most of the time, it's not storming.
The big exception was the Great Depression. It started in nineteen twenty nine, and the economy shrank for forty three months straight.
By nineteen thirty three, about one in four American workers had no job.
Back then, there was no unemployment insurance, and no deposit insurance for bank accounts. Thousands of banks failed. Many of today's safety nets were built because of that disaster.
So can we see a recession coming? Sometimes. Economists watch for warning signs.
The most famous one has a scary name. The inverted yield curve. Don't worry, it's simple.
Normally, if you lend money for a long time, you get paid more interest. Lending to the government for ten years should pay more than lending for three months. Makes sense. You're waiting longer.
But sometimes, it flips. Short loans pay more than long ones. That's an inverted yield curve.
It's like investors saying: we expect trouble ahead, and we expect interest rates to be cut. So let's lock in today's rate for ten years.
Since the late nineteen sixties, this curve flipped before every American recession.
But it's not perfect. It flipped in twenty twenty two and stayed upside down for about two years. And no recession came. It's a smoke alarm, not a crystal ball.
Other signs: more people asking for unemployment benefits, companies cutting hours, and big purchases like couches slowing down. Dave, take notes.
So what can Dave do? Here are some ideas. Education, not advice.
One. Build an emergency fund. Many experts suggest three to six months of living costs, saved in a safe account. It's a cushion for a hard landing.
Two. Keep learning skills. In a recession, people with skills that many companies need usually find work faster. Dave is learning online sales, just in case.

Three. Don't panic sell. In the two thousand eight crash, the S and P five hundred fell about fifty seven percent. People who sold at the bottom locked in the loss. People who waited got back to even by twenty thirteen.
And four. Don't pile up debt when times feel shaky. A job loss plus big credit card bills is a scary mix. Remember the raccoon?
As for Dave? The store cut his hours for a while. But thanks to his emergency fund, he paid his rent, stayed calm, and kept his job.
So let's recap.
One. A recession is a big, broad drop in the economy that lasts months. Not just two bad quarters.
Two. It spreads like dominoes. Less spending means layoffs, and layoffs mean less spending.
Three. Recessions end, usually in about ten months. So build a cushion, keep learning, and don't panic.
